tr.title: Turkey
paragraphs: Turkey's olympiads are run by TÜBİTAK; since 2019 they are part of the TÜBİTAK Science Olympiads (Bilim Olimpiyatları).

Senior olympiad: a First Round of multiple-choice questions with five options (36 questions until 2013, 32 from 2014), then the national final (Second Round), held in December: six problems over two days. The year shown is the calendar year of the December round.
IMO Team Selection Test: six problems a year until 2008, nine from 2010. There is also an EGMO selection test of two days with three problems each.

Middle school: the national middle-school olympiad (Ulusal İlköğretim Matematik Olimpiyatı until 2012, then Ulusal Ortaokul Matematik Olimpiyatı) has a multiple-choice First Round (21 questions until 2009, 30 in 2010–2013, 32 from 2014; until 2009 also three written-answer problems) and a Second Round of four problems.

ua.title: Ukraine
paragraphs: The Ukrainian Mathematical Olympiad ends with a final (IV stage) with a paper for each grade. In grades 9, 10 and 11 the final has two days with four problems a day (problems 1–4 on day 1, 5–8 on day 2).
In 2020 the official final was cancelled and the jury ran an online final (20–21 July 2020); in 2022 no final was held.
The IMO team is chosen by a Team Selection Test: four tests of three problems in 2015–2018.
The problems are published by the jury (matholymp.com.ua) and, in recent years, in the yearly books of the Junior Academy of Sciences (MAN).

ru.title: Russia
paragraphs: All-Russian Olympiad: an all-Russian olympiad was held in 1961–1966; from 1967 to 1991 it was replaced by the All-Union (USSR) olympiad. The All-Russian final stage was first held in 1993 (Anapa); there was none in 1992, and the 2020 final was cancelled. The final has two days of four problems for each of grades 9, 10 and 11.
Before the final comes the regional stage. Since 2009 its paper is set nationally: two days, 4 + 4 problems until 2017 and 5 + 5 from 2018.
Moscow Mathematical Olympiad: first held in 1935; 89 olympiads up to 2026 (none in 1942–1944). Since 1993 grades 8, 9 and 10 have six problems each.
St. Petersburg (Leningrad) Mathematical Olympiad: a city round and, until 2008, a selection (final) round; the selection round was abolished in 2009. Its year is the end of the school year.

ro.title: Romania
paragraphs: The Romanian National Mathematical Olympiad (ONM) has a final stage for each grade from 7 to 12, with four problems per grade.
It was not held in 2020 (COVID-19); in 2021 the Romanian Mathematical Society (SSMR) ran the national final as the "Olimpiada Națională Gazeta Matematică".
The IMO team is chosen by selection tests (baraj). In 1989–1993 there were also separate selection papers for the Balkan MO.
Papers are published by the SSMR (from 2012) and by the Ministry of Education archive (from 2003).

hu.title: Hungary
paragraphs: Hungary has the oldest mathematics competition still running. The Eötvös Competition was founded in 1894 for students who had just finished secondary school: three problems on the school curriculum. It continues today as the Kürschák Competition (three problems in five hours, detailed proofs).

OKTV, the National Secondary School Academic Competition of the Ministry of Education, began as a mathematics competition in 1923. It has three categories by the number of mathematics lessons a week in the student's school; category III is for special mathematics classes.

Since 1894 the journal KöMaL has run a monthly problem-solving competition for secondary-school students. For university students there is the Miklós Schweitzer Competition, founded in 1949 (in the bank's Undergraduate section).
The bank holds the Eötvös Competition 1894–1943, the Kürschák Competition from 1947 and OKTV papers from 2006.

rs.title: Serbia
paragraphs: Mathematics competitions in Serbia are run by the Mathematical Society of Serbia. The first secondary-school competition was held by its Belgrade branch in 1958, and the first Republic competition on 26 April 1959.

Students pass through county and regional competitions to the Republic (state) competition. Since 2007 the Serbian Mathematical Olympiad is the final stage, and the IMO team is chosen there and at selection tests.

Yugoslavia hosted the IMO twice, the second time in Belgrade in 1977. Yugoslav and later Serbian teams have taken part in the Balkan MO since 1987. Serbia hosted the Junior Balkan MO in 2004 (Novi Sad) and 2015 (Belgrade).
The bank holds the Serbian MO from 2007 and the Serbian IMO selection tests.

bg.title: Bulgaria
paragraphs: The Bulgarian National Mathematical Olympiad is one of the oldest in Europe. Before 1990 it had four rounds: school, regional, national and selection. Since 1990 it has three rounds: municipal, district and national. For the national round all qualified students meet in one place, usually Sofia.

The national round follows the IMO format: two days, three problems a day, ordered by increasing difficulty. Its problems are set by the national committee and are well known for their originality and technical difficulty.
Bulgaria also has the Winter and Spring mathematical competitions, held in different towns. The IMO team is chosen by a selection test after the national round.
The bank holds the national olympiad from 1962 and the selection tests.

br.title: Brazil
paragraphs: The Brazilian Mathematical Olympiad (OBM) is organised by the Brazilian Mathematical Society (SBM). Since 1998 it has three phases and three levels: Level 1 for grades 5–6, Level 2 for grades 7–8 and Level 3 for secondary school. The first phase is open to every interested student.
In 2005 the SBM started a second, much larger olympiad for public schools, OBMEP, with the government. By 2014 it reached about 19 million students a year in three levels and two stages.
The bank holds the OBM final (Level 3) from 1979, Level 2 from 1998, and Brazilian IMO selection tests.

pe.title: Peru
paragraphs: The Peruvian Mathematical Society took up the olympiads in 1988, when Lima hosted the 3rd Iberoamerican Mathematical Olympiad. Peru has taken part in the IMO since 1987, the Iberoamerican Olympiad since 1985 and the Cono Sur Olympiad since 1993.

The national olympiad, ONEM, was first held in 2001 in 5 cities with about 500 students. Since 2004 it has been run with the Ministry of Education, and more than a million students take its first round.

ONEM is for grades 7–11. It has four rounds: school, education unit, region (about 2,400 students) and a three-day national final in Lima (about 300 students). Public and private schools compete in separate categories (Alfa and Beta).
The bank holds Peruvian IMO selection test papers from 2009.

mn.title: Mongolia
paragraphs: The Mongolian Mathematical Olympiad (MMO) officially started in 1965; Mongolia first took part in the IMO in 1964. It is run by the Mongolian Mathematical Olympiad Committee. S. Urjintseren, one of the first Mongolian algebraists, chaired the national committee for 17 years.

The olympiad has several rounds, with separate papers for each grade and a category for teachers. The national final was the IV round from the 1980s to 2017, the III round in 1991–1992 and from 2018. It has two days of three problems.

The bank holds the senior problems of 1965–1985 and the national-final paper of the top school grade from 1986. Most of them come from the committee's yearly booklets, in English with the Mongolian original.

am.title: Armenia
paragraphs: Mathematical olympiads started in Armenia in 1952. Lecturers and instructors of the mechanics and mathematics department of Yerevan State University organised them, first for the city of Yerevan and later for the whole of Armenia. The first olympiads had 200 to 250 pupils from forms 6 to 10. They solved 4 or 5 problems in three hours.

Republican olympiads for schoolchildren started in 1961. The first was sponsored by the Ministry of Education of Armenia and Yerevan State University, for forms 5 to 11. They have three rounds: school, local and republican (as of 1991). The school-round problems are chosen by the school authorities and the local-round problems by the republican judges. The final round is held in Yerevan.
The journal Mathematics and Physics at School has been published since 1966 and regularly prints the problems of the second and third rounds (as of 1991).
The bank holds the Armenian national final from 2009.

at.title: Austria
paragraphs: The Austrian Mathematical Olympiad began in 1968, when Austria was invited to the IMO in Moscow and sent an observer. Special training courses were then set up in schools, taught mostly by school teachers. After a qualifying round, the first competition was held on 22 June 1970, and an eight-member team took part in the IMO in Keszthely that summer. Austria hosted the IMO in Lienz in 1976, with 19 teams.

The main competition has three rounds (as of 1997). The first is a course competition held in the preparatory courses around the end of April. The second is a regional competition held in May in three regions, with the same problems everywhere. The final round is held in June, over two days with three problems and four hours each day. At most 30 students qualify for it.

A separate Beginners' Round exists for students who are new to the olympiad and not yet in their final school year. It has a course round and a provincial round, and the provincial round is the final one. Before the final round there is a two-week preparatory seminar. It is also the training camp for the IMO team and for the team of the Austrian-Polish Mathematics Competition, which has been held since 1978.
The bank holds the Austrian final round from 1970 and the regional round from 2015.

cz.title: Czech Republic and Slovakia
paragraphs: In Czechoslovakia the Mathematical Olympiad is the oldest mathematics competition. It started about 40 years before the article, that is around 1951. In 1991 it had 8 categories, from the 4th grade of basic school (age 10) to the 4th grade of secondary school (age 18). A special category P, for programming, exists at secondary level.

In each category the pupils pass through several rounds, starting with a school round and ending with regional, county or national rounds. In each round they solve 3 or 4 problems in 3 to 4 hours. The national round of the highest category A lasts two days. The pupils solve 2 x 3 problems in 2 x 4 hours (as of 1991).

The best pupils of each category are invited to special meetings of one or two weeks with a scientific programme. Besides the olympiad there are correspondence seminars, which send problem sets by mail to pupils aged 10 to 18. In 1991 there were about 15 to 20 of them, run locally. The article was written just after the political changes of November 1989, which reduced the funding of some competitions.
The bank holds the national round of category A from 1952.

lv.title: Latvia
paragraphs: The article describes the competition system of Latvia over about 35 years. The problems of the school, regional, state and Open olympiads are prepared at the University of Latvia. The levels are as follows (as of 2004). The school level covers grades 5 to 12, and about 30 percent of pupils take part. The regional level covers grades 5 to 12 and has about 12,000 pupils in 39 places.

The state level is for grades 9 to 12. It is held at the University of Latvia over two consecutive days, and only those who do well on the first day take part on the second. Each region, each major city and each district of Riga sends at least 4 participants. The first-prize winners of the previous year may come too, and the total is about 330. A selection round for the IMO is held in April over two days, with about 15 participants.

The Latvian Open Mathematical Olympiad has been organised since 1974. It is held on the last Sunday of April for grades 5 to 12, and foreign teams also take part. In 2004 it had about 3,300 participants. In the school, regional and Open olympiads, one problem for each grade is taken from an olympiad of the two previous years.
The bank holds the grade 12 paper of the state olympiad from 1990.

ph.title: Philippines
paragraphs: The Philippine Mathematical Olympiad (PMO) grew out of the Metro Manila Mathematics Competition, which the Mathematical Society of the Philippines had run since 1976. In 1983 the minister of the National Science and Technology Authority supported turning it into a nationwide competition. The PMO was launched in 1984 as a joint project of that authority, the Ministry of Education, Culture and Sports and the Mathematical Society. A trial run took place in two regions in 1984, and the nationwide PMO started in 1986-87.

In 1992 the PMO had three stages: divisional, regional and national, over 14 regions. The divisional test, for all four high-school years, had 40 multiple-choice questions. Third- and fourth-year students went on to the regional stage, with an individual round of 6 problems in two hours and a team round of quick-answer questions.

The national stage was held in Manila, with individual rounds of 4 problems requiring full solutions and team rounds of 10 short questions; at that time the PMO was held every two years. The national finalists of 1986–87 formed the team for the 1988 IMO, the first time the Philippines took part.
The bank holds the national stage of the PMO from 2008.

pt.title: Portugal
paragraphs: Mathematical competitions in Portugal began in 1980 with a Mini-Olympiad in the central part of the country, started by the Portuguese Mathematical Society. By 1983 it had become a National Olympiad with schools from all over the country. It has been organised annually since then by the Portuguese Mathematical Society. A Pre-Olympiad was added in 1989 for pupils in Year 7.

The National Olympiad has two categories (as of 1992). Category A is for Years 8 and 9. Category B is for Years 10 to 12. The country is divided into three regions: North, Centre and South, and Islands. The first step is an eliminating test in every enrolled school. The second step is a test in some regional schools, which picks the 10 best students of each region for the final round.

The final round is held each year in a different town. It has a first part of 3 problems in two hours in the morning and a second part of 2 problems in the afternoon. Since 1989, the top 6 of category B have been selected to take part in the IMO. They receive special training for a week in June. In 1990 the participants numbered 22,958 in total.
The bank holds the final round of category B from 1994.

es.title: Spain
paragraphs: The first Spanish Mathematical Olympiad (OME) was held in 1964. It is organised annually by the Royal Spanish Mathematical Society (RSME) and sponsored by the Ministry of Education. The contestants (as of 1988) are pupils of the final pre-university year, the Curso de Orientacion Universitaria.

The contest has two rounds, each with two sessions. The first round takes place in all university districts, with 8 problems. Up to three winners per district receive a scholarship for studying mathematics at university. The second round, for the first-round winners, takes place in Madrid, with 6 problems. From 1980 the first-round problems are proposed by the local juries of the university districts, and the RSME only proposes its own as a guide. The second-round problems are proposed by the RSME.

The six best contestants of the second round receive money awards and can form the Spanish team for the IMO. Spain has taken part in the IMO since 1983, and the dates of the OME are set so that the team can train before the IMO. From 1985 Spain has also taken part in the Iberoamerican Mathematical Olympiad.
The bank holds the final round from 1964.

vn.title: Vietnam
paragraphs: The Vietnamese national mathematical olympiad began in 1962. It was held for gifted pupils at the end of the first and second levels (forms 5 and 9) and the third level (form 12). The Ministry of Education organises it every year (as of 1989).

It has four stages. First, gifted pupils are discovered and fostered at the start of the school year. Then competitions in each district choose teams for forms 5 and 9. Next, competitions in each province choose provincial teams for forms 5, 9 and 12. The problems of those stages are proposed by local juries. The last stage is the National Mathematical Olympiad, with problems set by a national jury.

The national competition is held over two days. On each day the pupils solve three problems in three hours. There are individual prizes and collective prizes. Vietnam sent its first team to an IMO in 1974, the 16th IMO in the German Democratic Republic, with five participants.
The bank holds the national olympiad from 1962 and the Vietnamese IMO selection tests from 1985.

in.title: India
paragraphs: The first Indian National Mathematical Olympiad (INMO) was held on Sunday 7 September 1986. It was organised by the National Board for Higher Mathematics (NBHM), set up by the Department of Atomic Energy; a National Steering Committee had been formed in early 1985 to plan it.

That first olympiad had two stages. A regional screening test was held in February 1986, with a common three-hour paper for all fifteen regions. Each region could send at most 5 percent of its candidates, and no more than twenty, to the national paper, which was written at 25 centres.

The papers were marked at IIT Kanpur, and a merit list of 22 candidates was released on 1 October 1986. The top scorers were interviewed in Bombay in December 1986 and received scholarships. India's participation in the IMO was then being planned.
The bank holds the INMO from 1986, the Regional Mathematical Olympiad (RMO) from 1990, PRMO/IOQM papers and Indian IMO selection tests.

ir2.title: Iran
paragraphs: The first mathematics competition in Iran was held on 30 March 1972. The Iranian Mathematical Society began it for university students during the 4th National Mathematics Conference, with 24 participants from 6 universities. It has been held each year on 30 March at the place of the annual conference. In March 1986, 37 students from 12 universities took part.

A competition for high-school students started in Isfahan in 1983. The first National Mathematics Competition for high-school students was held in 1984 by the Iranian Mathematical Society. In March 1986, 98 students from 10 provinces took part. Since 1987 a unified Provincial Mathematics Competition has been held.

Iran has taken part in the IMO since 1987. Each year the team is made up of the best scorers of the Iranian Mathematics Competition (as of 1991). A problem-solving workshop is held for the team. A scholarship was set up for the 48 best scorers of the national competition.
The bank holds the second round of the Iranian olympiad from 1988, papers of the third round and Iranian IMO selection tests.

mx.title: Mexico
paragraphs: The first Mexican Mathematical Olympiad was held in 1987. It was started by the Mexican Mathematical Society (Sociedad Matematica Mexicana). It had three steps. Regional competitions had more than 2000 students. The National Competition was held during the 20th meeting of the Society in Xalapa, Veracruz, in November 1987. The 62 regional winners took part.

The National Competition followed the scheme of the IMO. On each of two consecutive days, four problems (instead of three) were given, to be solved in four and a half hours. Each problem was worth 10 points.

The 12 winners of the National Competition received special training in January 1988. The team for the IMO was selected after this training. The authors reported some difficulties with financing the first olympiad (article of 1990).
The bank holds the national final from 1987.
